project_phase: Phase 3 (governance). NEX-058 IMPLEMENTED: authentication assurance is now persisted and the `step-up` obligation is enforced from evidence. `AuthenticationAssurance` is a closed, ordered vocabulary with floor semantics; absent or unrecognised values parse to single-factor, so an unpersisted value can never read as authority. The IdP-asserted level is recorded on the session at login, rehydrated into the Principal on resolve, and copied onto the delegation at grant, where it is fixed. The gateway compares that against STEP_UP_FLOOR, a static application constant a policy author cannot lower. Four of five named obligations now have real mechanisms; `step-up` has moved from designed to enforced. Remaining gaps: second-approver, risk-based approval.

The assurance columns are nullable and have exactly one writer each (login for sessions, grant for delegations). Any future writer must not default to multi-factor; `AuthenticationAssurance.parse` fails closed, but a SQL default of 'multi-factor' would bypass it entirely.

`step-up` is enforced against the delegator's assurance *at grant time*. A delegation granted at single-factor stays single-factor even if the human later steps up - they must re-grant. That is intentional (ADR-015) but will surprise an operator.
`second-approver` must be a distinct human, not a second click by the first approver. Reusing the first approver would make separation of duties a formality.

run_summary: Implemented NEX-058, the slice that turns ADR-015 from a design into a control. The previous run left step-up designed-but-refused, which was the honest state; this run makes it enforceable without ever letting a weaker check wear the obligation's name. The domain vocabulary is closed and ordered with floor semantics, and `parse()` fails closed to single-factor so an absent or unrecognised stored value degrades rather than escalates. The IdP's acr/amr claim is derived into that bounded vocabulary in the adapter, never carried as free text. Assurance is recorded on the session at login, rehydrated into the Principal on resolve, and copied onto the delegation at grant where it is fixed - because a delegation can outlive the session that created it, and consent is the moment the human chose. The gateway compares against STEP_UP_FLOOR, a static constant, so a policy author can ask for step-up but cannot define what counts as stepped up. Refusals are audited as denied invocations naming the obligation and the level actually held. Tests cover both directions: five persistence tests including absent-reads-as-single-factor, and a positive gateway case proving a multi-factor delegation satisfies the obligation - because an obligation that can only ever refuse is not enforced, it is merely unimplemented. Two test fixtures had to be repaired mid-run (a stale Harness API and a missing TOOL_GATEWAY import); both were real defects in the new test, not in the product code. Gates ran bare, as CI runs them: ruff format, ruff check, mypy over 139 files, and the full pytest suite, all green. CI itself was not polled - the clock ran out - so NEX-058 is recorded as completed but not VERIFIED.

decisions_this_run: D-058a: assurance is fixed onto the delegation at grant time, not read live from the session per call. A delegation can outlive the session that created it, and re-reading live would let an agent act under authority the human never held when they consented.

D-058b: STEP_UP_FLOOR is a static application constant, never read from a policy version. A policy author must be able to request step-up without being able to redefine what satisfies it, or the same rule that asks for the control could weaken it.

D-058c: `parse()` fails closed to single-factor rather than raising. A stored value a future build does not recognise must degrade to the weakest level, not crash an enforcement path or skip its check.
D-058d: a positive test was added alongside the refusal tests. The obligation was previously only provably refusable, which cannot distinguish 'enforced' from 'unimplemented'.
